# Statistical Methods {#sec-stats}

## Height-to-width ratio analysis

Height-to-width (h/w) ratios are computed from the bounding box of the largest
connected component of the binary silhouette mask (see §S2). For the physical
pixel-ratio analysis (used in the main paper ratio figures), ratios are derived
directly from image pixel dimensions. A separate pixel-ratio dataset drawn from
the CDLI preprocessed image archive (a larger subsample) provides corroboration.

All ratio analyses use the **natural log of the h/w ratio** (log-ratio) as the
primary analysis variable for statistical tests and diachronic trend estimation.
The log-ratio transformation is appropriate for proportional data because it is
symmetric around 0 (log-ratio of 0 corresponds to a square tablet), it corrects
the asymmetry inherent in raw ratio distributions (the portrait side spans 1 to ∞
while the landscape side spans 0 to 1), and it permits additive decomposition of
ratio shifts across multiplicative transformations of scale. Medians and IQR reported
in all tables are in the **original ratio scale** (not log-transformed) for readability.

**Diachronic trend** is assessed with Spearman rank correlation of period median
log-ratios against their chronological rank order (Uruk IV = rank 1,
Hellenistic = rank 21). Spearman ρ is used rather than Pearson *r* because
chronological rank, not calendar years, is the appropriate ordering variable:
the periods span very unequal time intervals, and the quantity of interest is
whether successive periods show monotonically decreasing h/w ratios, not the
rate of change per century.

**Between-period tests** use the Mann-Whitney *U* test (Wilcoxon rank-sum test)
for pairwise comparisons and the Kruskal-Wallis H test for omnibus evaluation.
These non-parametric tests are appropriate because h/w ratio distributions within
periods are substantially non-normal (right-skewed in portrait periods, left-skewed
in landscape periods). Effect sizes for pairwise comparisons are reported as
**Cliff's *δ*** (the probability that a randomly selected tablet from one group
has a higher h/w ratio than one from the other group, minus the reverse probability),
which has the advantage of being interpretable without assumptions about distributional
form and ranges from −1 (all group-2 values exceed group-1) to +1 (all group-1
values exceed group-2). By convention: |δ| < 0.147 = negligible; 0.147–0.330 = small;
0.330–0.474 = medium; > 0.474 = large.

**Standardization** is assessed via the **coefficient of variation** (CV = σ/μ)
of the h/w ratio within each period, following Eerkens & Bettinger [@eerkensStandardizationArtifact2000].
CV normalizes dispersion to the mean, permitting comparison of standardization
across periods with different absolute ratio levels. For the genre-stratified
standardization analysis (administrative tablets only), the same CV formula is
applied to the subset of tablets with CDLI genre label "Administrative."

**Confidence intervals** for period medians are bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000
resamples with replacement).

## VAE latent-space statistics

For each of the 12 VAE bottleneck dimensions, period discrimination is assessed
via the **Kruskal-Wallis H test** over the 21-period distribution of per-tablet
latent coordinates. Effect size is computed as:
$$\eta^2 = \frac{H - k + 1}{N - k}$$
where *H* is the Kruskal-Wallis statistic, *k* is the number of period groups,
and *N* is the total sample size. By convention: η² < 0.01 = small; 0.01–0.06 = medium;
> 0.06 = large.

Diachronic trend per VAE dimension is assessed with Spearman rank correlation
of per-period mean latent coordinates against chronological rank order (same ranks
as for ratio analysis). Significance is assessed at α = 0.05, two-tailed.

**Latent traversal analysis.** For each of three target dimensions (X2, X7, X8),
a traversal is constructed by:

1. Computing the genre-specific global mean vector over all tablets in the target
   genre (Administrative, Literary, or Legal).
2. Constructing 11 synthetic vectors that vary the target dimension from
   −2σ to +2σ (where σ is the global standard deviation of that dimension across
   all tablets), holding all other dimensions at the genre mean.
3. Decoding each synthetic vector through the VAE decoder to produce an 80×80
   pixel binary silhouette.
4. Measuring five geometric descriptors on each decoded image:
   - **h/w ratio**: height divided by width of the bounding box.
   - **Area fraction**: foreground pixel count divided by bounding-box area.
   - **Solidity**: foreground pixel count divided by convex hull area.
   - **Compactness**: 4π × area / perimeter².
   - **Eccentricity**: eccentricity of the ellipse fitted to the largest connected component.
5. Normalizing each descriptor 0–1 over the 11 traversal steps.
6. Identifying the **primary descriptor** as the one with the highest absolute
   Spearman ρ between descriptor value and traversal step index.

The traversal is run separately for each of three genre baselines
(Administrative, Literary, Legal) to assess whether the dimension's physical
interpretation is consistent across scribal traditions.

## Geographic analysis

**Zone assignment.** Each tablet with a non-uncertain provenience string is
matched to an archaeological site via the CDLI catalogue provenience field.
Site-to-region assignments are obtained from the CDLI Linked Open Data geographic
ontology (see §S5 for full methodology). The 19 CDLI-defined regions are
aggregated into 5 analytical zones: Southern Mesopotamia; Central/Northern
Babylonia; Assyria/Upper Mesopotamia; Elam/Western Iran; Periphery.
Tablets with the provenience string "uncertain (mod. uncertain)" or the flag
`is_provenience_uncertain = True` in the CDLI catalogue are excluded from all
geographic analyses but retained in all other analyses.

**Variance decomposition.** The overall log-ratio shift between the 2nd-millennium
and 1st-millennium subsamples is decomposed into:
$$\text{Overall shift} = \underbrace{\sum_z \frac{n_{z,2}}{N_2} \cdot \Delta_z}_{\text{within-zone}} + \underbrace{\text{Overall} - \text{Within}}_{\text{compositional}}$$
where $\Delta_z$ is the within-zone log-ratio shift for zone *z*, $n_{z,2}$
is the 2nd-millennium tablet count in zone *z*, and $N_2$ is the total
2nd-millennium tablet count with zone assignment. The within-zone component
captures real change in h/w ratio at production sites active in both millennia;
the compositional component captures how much of the overall shift would result
from the changing geographic composition of the corpus even if h/w ratios had
not changed at all within zones.

**Site-level tests.** Sites with a minimum of 30 tablets in both the 2nd-millennium
(Early Old Babylonian, Old Babylonian, Old Assyrian, Middle Assyrian, Middle
Babylonian, Middle Elamite, Hittite) and 1st-millennium (Neo-Assyrian, Neo-Babylonian,
Achaemenid, Hellenistic) subsamples are included in the site-level panel. Pairwise
comparisons use Mann-Whitney *U* with Cliff's *δ* as effect size. Bonferroni
correction is applied across the set of tested sites (*n* = 10; corrected α = 0.005).

# Silhouette Extraction Pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

## Image preprocessing

Raw CDLI photographs vary substantially in background colour, illumination angle,
scale bar presence, and resolution. The following preprocessing pipeline was
applied uniformly to all 94,936 images:

1. **Grayscale conversion.** All images are converted to single-channel grayscale
   (weighted sum: 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B).

2. **Colorbar removal.** CDLI images frequently include a colour reference bar
   (grayscale or Munsell colour scale) along one edge. These are detected and
   removed using a template-matching procedure that identifies the characteristic
   horizontal stripe pattern. Code: notebook `1.1 preprocess - remove colorbar.ipynb`.

3. **Otsu thresholding** [@otsuThresholdSelectionMethod1979]. A globally optimal
   binary threshold is computed from the grayscale histogram using Otsu's
   criterion, which maximizes inter-class variance between foreground (tablet)
   and background pixels. The resulting binary mask separates the clay body from
   the photographic background.

4. **Morphological closing.** A 3×3 structuring element is applied with morphological
   closing (dilation followed by erosion) to fill small holes caused by surface
   engraving, clay damage, or high-frequency texture. This prevents fragmentation
   of the tablet silhouette in heavily inscribed areas.

5. **Largest connected component.** The connected components of the binary mask are
   extracted. The component with the largest foreground pixel count is retained as
   the tablet silhouette; all smaller components (scale bars, reflections, label
   tags) are discarded.

6. **Bounding box and ratio.** The height-to-width ratio is computed from the
   bounding box of the retained component. For classifier training, the silhouette
   is rescaled to 80×80 pixels.

## Known limitations of the pipeline

**Composite images.** A subset of CDLI photographs shows multiple tablet faces
(obverse, reverse, and lateral edges) on a single canvas in a composite layout.
For such images, the largest connected component may capture either a single face
or a merged shape spanning multiple faces, depending on the gap between faces.
This introduces a potential systematic bias in the h/w ratio of composite images
(the merged silhouette is wider than any individual face), and may contribute to
the VAE X8 dimension's apparent decrease over time (composite multi-face photography
is more prevalent in later CDLI submissions). This confound is explicitly discussed
in the main text (§3.3, X8 interpretation).

**Scale-dependent ratio stability.** Because the pipeline works with pixel ratios
rather than physical dimensions, the computed h/w ratio is invariant to camera
distance and image resolution — a property required for the analysis. However,
it is also insensitive to actual tablet size, meaning a 3 cm letter and a 30 cm
archival record that share the same proportions are indistinguishable by this
measure.

# Model Architectures and Training {#sec-models}

## Decision tree baseline

A single CART decision tree is trained on the scalar h/w ratio as its only feature,
predicting 21-class period labels. Training uses the same 80/20 stratified split
as all other classifiers. This model establishes the minimum performance achievable
with the simplest possible shape descriptor.

## Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)

Architecture: three convolutional blocks (Conv2D → BatchNorm → ReLU → MaxPool),
followed by two fully connected layers (512 → 256 → 21), trained on masked
80×80 binary silhouettes. Cross-entropy loss, Adam optimiser (lr = 0.001),
batch size 64, 30 epochs. Training code: notebooks `6–7.1`.

## ResNet50

Architecture: ResNet50 [@heResNet2016] with ImageNet pretrained weights, final
fully connected layer replaced with a 21-class classification head. Fine-tuned
end-to-end. Input: 3-channel 224×224 images (grayscale images replicated across
channels; masked silhouettes similarly replicated). Cross-entropy loss, Adam
optimiser with cosine learning rate schedule, batch size 32, 30 epochs.

**Two experimental conditions:**
- *Grayscale condition*: full photographic image, normalized with ImageNet statistics.
- *Masked silhouette condition*: binary mask replicated to 3 channels, normalized
  with binary-image statistics.

Training code: notebooks `8–9.1`. The shape information retention fraction
(61%/71% ≈ 0.86) is computed as the ratio of masked to grayscale macro-F1.

## DINOv2 feature extraction and classification

A pretrained DINOv2 ViT-B/14 model [@oquabDINOv22023] was used for visual feature
extraction (1024-dimensional embedding per image), followed by an XGBoost classifier.
This pipeline was evaluated on both grayscale and masked conditions. Training code:
notebooks `3–4.1`. DINOv2+XGBoost performance is not the primary comparison in the
main paper but provides an additional benchmark in the three-method comparison.

## Variational Autoencoder (VAE)

**Architecture:**

- *Encoder*: three convolutional blocks (32 → 64 → 128 channels), followed by two
  fully connected branches producing μ (12-dimensional) and log-σ² (12-dimensional).
- *Bottleneck*: 12-dimensional Gaussian latent space; reparameterization trick.
- *Decoder*: fully connected layer (12 → 512), followed by three transposed
  convolutional blocks (128 → 64 → 32 → 1 channel), sigmoid output.
- *Classification head*: fully connected branch from the 12-dimensional latent vector
  to 21-class softmax output (auxiliary classification loss; weight β = 1.0 relative
  to reconstruction loss).

**Training:** 94,936 masked 80×80 binary silhouettes; batch size 8; Adam
optimiser, lr = 0.0001; 30 epochs (best checkpoint at epoch 22, step 213,621).
Combined loss: β-VAE reconstruction + KL divergence + classification cross-entropy.
Class weights were computed from the inverse of per-period frequency to compensate
for class imbalance, using equal-partition re-weighting.

**Availability:** Trained model checkpoint and class weights are available on
Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11668219). Latent encodings for all 94,936 tablets
are included in the main dataset release (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.12787745).

Training code: notebook `10. train_VAE model - masked tablets.ipynb`.
Encoding extraction: notebook `10.1 extract VAE encodings.ipynb`.

(η² > 0.15): X7, X12, X6, X4. The dissociation between discrimination and trend

## Physical interpretation of the three significant dimensions

**X7 — Height/Width ratio (diplomatic-tradition axis).** Confirmed as the
primary descriptor for all three genre baselines (Administrative, Literary, Legal).
Moving from high X7 (+4) to low X7 (−4), the decoded silhouette transitions from a
tall, narrow portrait form to a wide, compact landscape form. The dimension
discriminates scribal traditions non-monotonically in time: Neo-Assyrian (X7 = +2.05)
and ED I-II (X7 = +1.86) are both portrait extremes; Achaemenid (X7 = −2.48) and
Middle Babylonian (X7 = −1.79) are landscape extremes. The 3rd-millennium mean
(periods 1–9) and 1st-millennium mean (periods 17–21) differ by only 0.075 on X7,
confirming the absence of linear temporal trend.

**X2 — Bounding-box fill efficiency (diachronic-drift axis).** Primary descriptor is
area fraction for Administrative and Legal genres; solidity for Literary tablets.
Moving from low X2 (−5) to high X2 (+4), the decoded silhouette transitions from
a tall, narrow portrait shape with articulated outline to a wide, compactly rectangular
form that fills its bounding box efficiently. The 3rd-millennium administrative mean
(X2 = −0.995) differs from the 1st-millennium administrative mean (X2 = +0.652)
by Δ = +1.647, representing the combined portrait-to-landscape rotation and outline
regularization of the diachronic trend. The genre inconsistency of the primary
descriptor (area fraction vs. solidity) reflects the different ways in which
"efficient bounding-box use" manifests across scribal traditions.

**X8 — Body unity / silhouette cohesion (secondary diachronic axis).** Primary
descriptor is solidity for All tablets, Literary, and Legal; area fraction for
Administrative. Moving from high X8 (+3) to low X8 (−3), the decoded silhouette
transitions from a segmented, articulated outline to a unified, slab-like form.
The 3rd-millennium mean (−0.099 all-tablet; −0.144 administrative) differs from
the 1st-millennium mean (−0.291 all-tablet; −0.660 administrative), reflecting
a progressive unification of tablet outlines across time. The 3rd- and 1st-millennium
marks (−0.25 and −0.85 on the traversal axis) fall in the lower half of the ±2σ
range, indicating that the historical variation in X8 represents a moderate fraction
of the full dynamic range of this dimension.

# Geographic Region Methodology and Supplementary Table S-Geo {#sec-geo}

## Data sources

Geographic region assignments follow a three-source hierarchy:

**1. CDLI catalogue (`artifacts.csv`).** Provenience information is taken directly
from the CDLI catalogue export. Each tablet's provenience is recorded as a free-text
string in canonical CDLI format, e.g., "Nippur (mod. Nuffar)". The ancient site
name is extracted by stripping the modern-toponym parenthetical.

**2. CDLI Linked Open Data — `places.nt`.** The file `places.nt` is an RDF
N-Triples export from the CDLI Linked Open Data (LOD) infrastructure (cdli.network).
It encodes 737 named provenience entities and, for 245 of them, an explicit region
assignment via the CIDOC-CRM spatial containment predicate `P89_falls_within`.
Each provenience entity is linked to one of 19 CDLI-defined geographic regions.
The CDLI LOD geographic ontology is grounded in Pleiades — an open, peer-reviewed
gazetteer of ancient places.

**3. Manual supplement for unmatched sites.** A small number of high-frequency
sites in the 2nd–1st millennium corpus are absent from the `places.nt` region
assignments. These are assigned manually by the authors following standard
historical-geographic references (Roaf 1990; Radner & Robson 2011).

| Site (CDLI label) | Manual region | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Puzriš-Dagan | Southern Mesopotamia | Steinkeller (1987); Sigrist (1992) |
| Ḫattusa | Western and Central Anatolia | Bryce (2005) |
| Ešnunna | Central Mesopotamia | Hamblin (2006) |
| Garšana | Southern Mesopotamia | Owen & Mayr (2007) |
| Pārśa (Persepolis) | Eastern Iran | Brosius (2006) |

: **Table S5.** Manual region assignments for high-frequency sites absent from
  the CDLI LOD region ontology.

## The 19 CDLI regions and 5 analytical zones

| Analytical Zone | CDLI Regions Included |
|---|---|
| Southern Mesopotamia | Southern Mesopotamia |
| Central / N. Babylonia | Central Mesopotamia, Middle Euphrates |
| Assyria / Upper Mesopotamia | Tigridian Region, Jazirah |
| Elam / Western Iran | Western Iran, Eastern Iran |
| Periphery | W. & C. Anatolia, N. Levant, S. Levant, Upper Euphrates |

: **Table S6.** Aggregation of the 19 CDLI geographic regions into 5 analytical
  zones. Zone boundaries follow historical-geographic reference works (Roaf 1990;
  Radner & Robson 2011). The remaining 9 CDLI regions (Cyprus, Lower Egypt,
  Upper Egypt, Eastern Arabia, Western Mediterranean, Eastern Mediterranean,
  Arabian Peninsula, South Caucasus, and several minor regions) contribute fewer
  than 100 tablets to the 2nd–1st millennium subsample and are classified as
  Periphery if covered, or excluded otherwise.

## Limitations of the geographic analysis

1. **places.nt coverage**: Of 737 provenience entities in the CDLI LOD ontology,
   only 245 carry region assignments (33%). Coverage is good for the major excavated
   sites but sparse for smaller or uncertain proveniences. Tablets with unresolved
   provenience are excluded from the geographic analysis.

2. **2nd-millennium definition**: The 2nd-millennium subsample uses CDLI period
   labels Early Old Babylonian, Old Babylonian, Old Assyrian, Middle Assyrian,
   Middle Babylonian, Middle Elamite, and Hittite. The 1st-millennium subsample
   uses Neo-Assyrian, Neo-Babylonian, Achaemenid, and Hellenistic. Periods
   straddling the boundary (some Middle Babylonian tablets date to the late
   12th–11th centuries BCE) are assigned by CDLI period label, not by exact date.

3. **Uruk sampling imbalance**: Uruk contributes 235 tablets in the 2nd-millennium
   subsample and 4,923 in the 1st millennium (a 21-fold ratio). The variance
   decomposition is designed to test whether this imbalance drives the corpus-level
   trend (see §S1.3 and main text §3.5).

# Code Repository and Notebook Guide {#sec-notebooks}

## Overview

All analyses in this paper are implemented as Jupyter notebooks in Python.
The full repository is available at:
**https://github.com/DigitalPasts/ShapingHistory**

The notebooks are organized into three groups:

- **Data pipeline** (notebooks 0–2): acquire, preprocess, and explore the corpus
- **Analysis** (notebooks 2.1–2.6, 2.4b): statistical and visual analyses
  reported in the paper
- **ML models** (notebooks 3–13): train, evaluate, and interpret machine learning models

An interactive web companion to this paper — providing static rendered versions of
all notebooks and live access to the VAE traversal and interpolation widgets — is
available at:
**https://digitalpasts.github.io/ShapingHistory**

## Data pipeline notebooks

| Notebook | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `0. get and preprocess CDLI tabular data.ipynb` | Download CDLI catalogue; extract physical dimensions, period/genre labels, and provenience strings; save to `artifacts.csv`. Run once only. |
| `1. scrape tablet photos by era.ipynb` | Download CDLI tablet photographs by period. Requires CDLI API access. |
| `1.1 preprocess - remove colorbar.ipynb` | Detect and remove CDLI colour reference bars from raw photographs using template matching. |

## Analysis notebooks

These notebooks are the primary computational outputs of the paper. They are designed
to be run in sequence; notebooks 2.4 and later depend on data and figures produced
by earlier notebooks.

| Notebook | Paper section | Key outputs |
|---|---|---|
| `2.1 EDA - height-weight ratio of tablets.ipynb` | §Results 3.1 | Period-level h/w distributions, preliminary plots |
| `2.2 Statistical Analysis and Figure Export.ipynb` | §Results 3.1–3.2 | Fig. 1–2 (ratio distribution, diachronic trend, CV standardization); `period_summary_stats.csv` |
| `2.3 CV Pixel Ratio Analysis.ipynb` | §Results 3.1, SI §S4 | Image-derived pixel ratios; `pixel_ratio_summary_stats.csv`; SI Table S4 |
| `2.4 VAE Shape Feature Analysis.ipynb` | §Results 3.3 | Fig. 3 (η² vs ρ); `vae_dim_stats.csv`; `vae_period_mean_vectors.csv`; genre trajectories |
| `2.4b VAE Geometric Shape Analysis.ipynb` | §Results 3.3–3.4 | Fig. 4 (traversal filmstrips); Fig. 5 (dendrogram); descriptor trend figures; primary descriptor tables |
| `2.5 Three-Method Comparison.ipynb` | §Results 3.1–3.3 | Side-by-side comparison of physical ratio, pixel ratio, and VAE top dimension; SI figures |
| `2.6 Geographic Regional Analysis.ipynb` | §Results 3.5; SI §S5 | Fig. 6 (maps); zone-shift figures; variance decomposition; `supplementary_table_S_Geo.csv` |

## Machine learning model notebooks

| Notebook | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `5–5.1` | Decision tree on h/w ratio (baseline classifier) |
| `6–6.1` | CNN period classifier, grayscale images |
| `7–7.1` | CNN period classifier, masked silhouettes |
| `8–8.1` | ResNet50 period classifier, grayscale images |
| `9–9.1` | ResNet50 period classifier, masked silhouettes |
| `3–3.1` | DINOv2 feature extraction + classification, grayscale |
| `4–4.1` | DINOv2 feature extraction + classification, masked |

## Interactive visualization notebooks

Two notebooks provide the interactive VAE exploration tools described in
§Results 3.4 (Widget case study):

| Notebook | Description |
|---|---|
| `12. Traverse the VAE latent space.ipynb` | **Feature explorer widget.** Select a period and genre; the widget displays period mean vectors and per-dimension boxplots. Use the sliders to adjust individual dimensions and observe the decoded tablet silhouette in real time. Requires the trained VAE model (auto-downloaded from Zenodo on first run). |
| `13. Traversing the latent space between two images.ipynb` | **Interpolation widget.** Select two tablets (or specify two latent vectors); the widget decodes and displays the morphological path between them in 11 steps. Supports the case study in §Results 3.4. |

**Running the interactive widgets locally:**

```bash
# 1. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/DigitalPasts/ShapingHistory.git
cd ShapingHistory

# 2. Create environment
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 3. Launch Jupyter
jupyter notebook

# 4. Open notebook 12 or 13.
#    On first run, the VAE model is downloaded automatically from Zenodo
#    (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11668219, ~87 MB).
#    VAE encodings are downloaded from Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.12787745.
```

**Running via Binder (no local installation required):**

Click the Binder badge on the repository landing page, or navigate to:
`https://mybinder.org/v2/gh/DigitalPasts/ShapingHistory/HEAD`

Note: Binder sessions are ephemeral; downloaded model files are not persisted
between sessions.

# Data and Code Availability {#sec-data}

**CDLI Catalogue.** Provenience, period, genre, and physical dimension data are
obtained from the CDLI catalogue (cdli.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de), accessed 2024. The
catalogue is freely available under the CC BY 4.0 licence.

**Dataset release.** Extracted h/w ratios, image-derived pixel ratios, VAE latent
encodings (all 94,936 tablets × 12 dimensions), and all period/genre metadata are
available at:
Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.12787745

**Trained models.** The VAE model checkpoint (epoch 22, step 213,621) and training
configuration are available at:
Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11668219

**Code repository.** All Jupyter notebooks, analysis scripts, and this paper's
Quarto source are available at:
https://github.com/DigitalPasts/ShapingHistory

**Geographic data.** The `places.nt` CDLI Linked Open Data export is distributed
with the CDLI infrastructure (cdli.network) and is included in the code repository.
Natural Earth 110m country boundaries used for map figures are available from
Natural Earth (naturalearthdata.com) under the public domain.

**Interactive companion website.** An interactive web companion providing rendered
notebook outputs and live access to the VAE traversal and interpolation tools is
available at:
https://digitalpasts.github.io/ShapingHistory
